newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FOCUS-Asian bond issuers to offer more variety in 97.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Asian bond issuers to offer more variety in 97.

text.p: International fixed income investors can expect Asian debt issuers to provide more deals with longer maturities and in a wider variety of structures in 1997, bankers in Hong Kong said.

"The key factors I think would be increasing tenor of issues, more global structures to increase liquidity and also growth in domestic currency bond issues," said David Kenny, head of debt capital markets at HSBC Markets.
While Asian banks and corporations still rely heavily on bank loans, they are increasingly tapping the international capital markets as a way to diversify funding, bankers said.

"I think there is a growing realisation among Asian corporates that the bank markets are really only one source of financing and that they should look at the capital markets," said Chris van Niekerk, executive director at SBC Warburg.
By the middle of 1996, the volume of Asian bond issuance had already reached levels recorded for all of 1995, he noted.

Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand (IFCT) and India's Reliance Industries Ltd were the first to hit the international trail this year with long-dated issues sold to U.S. institutional investors last week. Some of the Reliance paper matures in 100 years.

"We're going to see much more longer-dated issuance in the markets of Asia, which will be a tremendous diversification for many borrowers away from the traditional bank sectors," predicted John McNiven, managing director at Merrill Lynch, which lead managed the IFCT and Reliance deals.

Bankers said they expect the U.S. dollar to remain the currency of choice for most Asian borrowers, though some issuers are likely to try other currencies, such as German marks, French francs, British sterling and Australian dollars.
International bond issues denominated in Asian currencies are also expected to become a bigger feature, aided by the gradual opening of Asian domestic markets to foreign investors.

"The Thai baht and the Indonesian rupiah markets have become more or less stable investment alternatives for international investors and they look like they are going to be joined fairly quickly by the Europeso market," said David Walker-Smith, senior vice president and head of debt capital markets at BA Asia.

Asian borrowers' funding costs declined in 1996 as foreign investors became more familiar with the improving credit story in Asia, but most still must pay a premium over similarly rated issuers in Europe to attract investors.
Bankers see spreads for Asian credits shrinking further in 1997, though the compression may not be as dramatic as in 1996.
With spreads narrowing, international investors are expected to buy longer-dated paper to eke out higher returns. They also will look more closely at lower rated borrowers, bankers said.

Investors will find there is more variety in terms of structured transactions as well, bankers said. "More and more (investment) houses are coming into the market and there are more experts in structured financings and securitised deals," said Phillip Cracknell, group head of syndicate and asset sales at Standard Chartered Bank.
Borrowers, meanwhile, will encounter a wider variety of investors in 1997. Traditionally conservative pension funds will vie with emerging market funds for Asian bonds, bankers said.
While bullish on Asian bonds in general, bankers said some of the big stories of 1996, notably the Philippines, will continue to play well in 1997. China also is grabbing attention.

Investors also are likely to hear more from Hong Kong, which up to now has been a relatively rare name in global debt markets. First out of the block will be Dao Heng Bank, which is planning a subordinated bond issue for later this month.
